text: The exhibit below was composed on 2026-09-14, in period voice. No such post exists in the 1995 archives. Every fact it jokes about is real; the post is not. The vault does not forge its evidence — it labels its fiction.

Told straight: in August 1995 Microsoft shipped Windows 95 to “Start Me Up”, lit the Empire State Building in its logo’s colours, and was, by every account including its own, the opposite of free software. Its founder’s first public act had been a 1976 letter informing hobbyists that most of them stole their software. Its revenue was the per-copy licence, the one thing free software by construction does not have. Linux was a four-year-old kernel on an FTP server in North Carolina; the phrase “open source” would not be coined for another two and a half years. The internet’s favourite joke about Microsoft that year was the acquisition hoax — the previous December a spoof wire story had the company buying the Catholic Church, complete with a Redmond spokesman, and it travelled far enough that Microsoft issued a real denial. Microsoft to become the world’s largest free-software maintainer was a headline in exactly that genre: funny because impossible. So here is the post that could have gone out that week, written with thirty-one years of hindsight and none of the vocabulary.
The exhibit

Path: news.helsinki.fi!news.funet.fi!anon.penet.fi!not-for-mail From: an314159@anon.penet.fi (Anonymous) Newsgroups: comp.os.linux.advocacy,comp.os.ms-windows.advocacy Subject: [PARODY] MICROSOFT TO BECOME WORLD'S LARGEST FREE SOFTWARE MAINTAINER Date: Fri, 25 Aug 1995 07:41:02 GMT Organization: Anonymous contact service Lines: 121 Message-ID: <41gk3s$pi7@anon.penet.fi> X-Anonymously-To: comp.os.linux.advocacy Someone left this on a BBS here in Helsinki last night, between the warez and a .WAV of Jay Leno. Forwarding for the group's amusement. It is obviously not real: Microsoft would sooner publish the source to Windows than admit that Linux exists. --- begin forwarded --- MICROSOFT TO BECOME WORLD'S LARGEST FREE SOFTWARE MAINTAINER "Where do you want to go today?" -- "/pub/Linux" REDMOND, Wash., Aug. 24 (AP) -- Hours after "Start Me Up" played for the last time and the last customer left the midnight line at the Bellevue Egghead, Microsoft Corp. chairman Bill Gates announced that the company will become, over the next quarter-century, the world's largest maintainer of free software, as measured by whoever ends up doing the counting. "In 1976 I wrote that most hobbyists steal their software," Gates told reporters, reading from the Open Letter to Hobbyists on a Windows 95 laptop that had not yet crashed. "We have decided to save them the trouble." Under the plan, the company that this week spent a reported $300 million teaching the public where the Start button is will: * Purchase sunsite.unc.edu and tsx-11.mit.edu, the two ftp sites where Linux lives, "so that the world's free software has a home it can never be evicted from, except by us." * Acquire Walnut Creek CDROM, so that every disc of free software in every bookstore in America is pressed by Microsoft. * Ship a complete copy of Linux inside a future version of Windows, "for compatibility with the future." The kernel will be built in Redmond. Source will be provided, as the licence requires, in a directory nobody looks in. * Submit more patches to Linus Torvalds than any other company on Earth, "until he accepts our hardware drivers." * Join Linux International as its largest dues-paying member, at whatever the top tier ends up being called. * Release the source code to MS-DOS the moment it becomes worthless, which the company estimates at around 2014. * Release the source code to the Windows Calculator, so that someone, somewhere, can finally make 3.11 minus 3.1 equal 0.01. * Give a future version of Windows away for nothing, on the theory that it is not the software you charge for. * Ship a free programmer's editor, source and all, that runs on Linux, and that more programmers will use than Emacs and vi put together. Mr. Stallman has been sent a copy. * Invent a programming language, give it away with the source, and watch it become one of the three most used languages on the ftp site it just bought -- alongside two free ones it did not write. * Rebuild Internet Explorer on a browser engine the company did not write. This will be the second browser Microsoft has not written, after the first. * Complete the GNU Hurd, which the Free Software Foundation has described as "coming soon" since 1990. Redmond estimates delivery in the first quarter of 1996. The company's lawyers, who have reviewed the GNU General Public License, describe it as "fine, actually," and have offered Microsoft's patents to anyone who would like them. Employment offers have gone out to the author of Python, a free scripting language named after a British comedy troupe, and to the founders of whatever free desktop environment gets written next. Richard Stallman could not be reached for comment. Sources at the Free Software Foundation say he was offered the title of Chief Evangelist and countered with "GNU/Microsoft." Linus Torvalds, reached at the University of Helsinki, said he had not read the announcement and would not be merging it. Chairman Gates was later photographed embracing a gnu. REACTION Netscape Communications Corp., whose shares have more than doubled since its public offering two weeks ago, dismissed the announcement. "What would we do -- give away our source code?" a spokesman said. IBM said it would not spend a billion dollars on a hobbyist operating system when it already has OS/2 Warp, and would certainly not spend thirty-four. Caldera Inc., a Utah company that sells Linux with a desktop on it, said it would sooner sue every Unix user in America than take Microsoft's money. Apple Computer could not be reached. A receptionist said the company was busy looking for an operating system. The Microsoft Network, which went live this morning, will continue to run on Windows NT "for the foreseeable future," a spokesman said. "We would never run our own service on free software." Microsoft's public relations department declined to deny the report, on the grounds that it had never heard of Linux. Microsoft shares fell 3 1/8 on the news and recovered 4 1/4 on the realization that it was a joke. Analysts said the market would revisit the question in about twenty years. --- end forwarded --- Anyway. Buy a bigger hard disk; Windows 95 wants 50 MB and your dignity. Kernel 1.2.13 still fits on a floppy. -- "640K ought to be enough for anybody." -- attributed, denied, repeated
The landlord

The 1995 reader’s nightmare was never that Microsoft might write free software. It was that Microsoft might own the place free software is kept — the parody’s bullet about the FTP sites is the one with teeth — and that is the gag that came true most completely. Since October 2018 Microsoft has owned GitHub, and GitHub is where the canonical repositories of Python (moved there in 2017), Rust, Node.js, Kubernetes, LLVM (2019), PyTorch, TensorFlow, React and Swift live, along with mirrors of Linux and Git and, since 2025, Firefox — the direct descendant of the code Netscape “would never” give away. Since 2020 it has owned npm, the largest package registry in the world, so that every npm install on Earth resolves against a Microsoft server; since 2019, Dependabot and CodeQL, which patrol dependencies and code across the platform. More than a hundred million developers keep their work there.

It also owns the most popular open-source tools on that platform, not just the platform. Visual Studio Code is the editor of just under three-quarters of the developers who answer Stack Overflow’s survey — more than Vim, Neovim and Emacs put together, which is the gag about Mr. Stallman’s copy. TypeScript, given away under Apache 2.0 from its first release in 2012, was one of the three most used languages on GitHub from 2022 to 2024, behind Python and JavaScript, and GitHub’s 2025 count reported it had become the first. Playwright, PowerToys, Windows Terminal, .NET and PowerShell are Microsoft’s; since May 2025 so are the source of the Windows Subsystem for Linux itself and of the Copilot Chat extension. And by GitHub’s own Octoverse, the open-source project with the most contributors in the world in 2018 — the year Microsoft bought GitHub — was microsoft/vscode; in 2019 Microsoft held the top two places. The counted became the counter.

The old guard declined the invitation: GNU keeps Savannah, Debian its own GitLab, GNOME and KDE theirs, and the kernel stays on kernel.org with GitHub as a mirror. Nearly everyone else moved in. Whether the landlord is a benevolent one is not this entry’s question — the vault records reversals, not verdicts — but of the three verbs the Halloween Documents made famous, embrace and extend are on the ledger below, and the third is a position still open, of the kind the vault files under futures.
The ledger
Hindsight loves to sharpen a joke, so every gag is checked against the record. Dates are the sources’; nothing below is rounded toward the punchline.
The gag, 1995
The record
The largest maintainer of free software, “as measured by whoever ends up doing the counting”

GitHub counted: in its 2016 Octoverse, Microsoft was the organisation with the most open-source contributors. In 2018 Microsoft bought the counter, for $7.5 billion. By that counter’s own Octoverse, the open-source project with the most contributors in 2018 was microsoft/vscode; in 2019 Microsoft held the top two places.
Recanting the Open Letter to Hobbyists — “we have decided to save them the trouble”
Windows 10 was a free upgrade for a year from July 2015. Visual Studio Code, .NET, TypeScript and PowerShell are free of charge and MIT- or Apache-licensed.
Buying the FTP sites where Linux lives

GitHub, announced 4 June 2018, closed that October: the largest host of source code in the world, home to the canonical repositories of Python, Rust, Node.js, Kubernetes, LLVM, PyTorch, TensorFlow, React, Swift and, since 2025, Firefox, and to mirrors of Linux and Git. Run from 2018 to 2021 by Nat Friedman, co-founder of Ximian, the first GNOME company.
Buying Walnut Creek CDROM, so every disc of free software is pressed by Microsoft
npm, Inc., acquired by GitHub in March 2020: the largest package registry in the world. Dependabot (May 2019) and Semmle’s CodeQL (September 2019) came first.
A complete Linux inside Windows, the kernel built in Redmond, source provided as the licence requires

Windows Subsystem for Linux, 2016. WSL 2 ships a Microsoft-built Linux kernel under the GPLv2 with the source on GitHub, 2019–2020. Microsoft also builds its own distribution, Azure Linux, born CBL-Mariner in 2020.
More patches to Linus than any other company, “until he accepts our hardware drivers”

July 2009: 20,000 lines of Hyper-V drivers submitted under the GPL. July 2011: by LWN’s count Microsoft was the top contributor to Linux 3.0 by changesets — almost all of it cleaning up those drivers.
Joining Linux International at “whatever the top tier ends up being called”
Platinum member of the Linux Foundation, 16 November 2016. The top tier is called Platinum.
MS-DOS source “the moment it becomes worthless, around 2014”
25 March 2014: MS-DOS 1.25 and 2.0, through the Computer History Museum. Re-released under MIT in 2018; MS-DOS 4.0 followed under MIT on 25 April 2024.
The Calculator’s source, so someone can fix it
Windows Calculator, MIT licence, 6 March 2019. Windows 3.1’s Calculator did famously display 3.11 minus 3.1 as 0.00.
A free editor, source and all, running on Linux, used by more programmers than Emacs and vi put together

Visual Studio Code, source under MIT since November 2015, on Linux from the start: the most used development environment in Stack Overflow’s 2023 and 2024 surveys, at just under three-quarters of respondents — more than Vim, Neovim and Emacs combined. The caveat the record insists on: Microsoft’s own binaries carry a proprietary licence, which is why VSCodium exists.
A language given away with its source, among the three most used on the FTP site it bought
TypeScript, Apache 2.0 from its first release on 1 October 2012: third on GitHub from 2022 to 2024 behind Python and JavaScript, and first by GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse.
Internet Explorer rebuilt on an engine Microsoft did not write — “the second browser Microsoft has not written, after the first”

IE 1.0 was licensed Spyglass Mosaic (1995). Edge was rebuilt on Chromium, Google’s open-source project, whose engine descends through WebKit from KDE’s KHTML: announced 6 December 2018, shipped 15 January 2020.
The lawyers finding the GPL “fine, actually”, and giving the patents away
Ballmer, 2001: Linux is “a cancer”. Ballmer, 2016: “now I love it”. Microsoft joined the Open Invention Network on 10 October 2018 and pledged its 60,000-plus patents to the Linux ecosystem.
Hiring the author of Python and “the founders of whatever free desktop environment gets written next”
Guido van Rossum joined Microsoft on 12 November 2020. GNOME was founded in 1997; its co-founder Miguel de Icaza arrived with the Xamarin acquisition in February 2016.
Gates photographed embracing a gnu
Satya Nadella, on stage in San Francisco, 20 October 2014, in front of a slide reading “Microsoft ♥ Linux”.
Netscape: “What would we do — give away our source code?”
Netscape did, announced 22 January 1998. The project was called Mozilla, and the term “open source” was coined twelve days later to describe what it had just done.
IBM: not a billion dollars on a hobbyist operating system, “and certainly not thirty-four”
IBM committed $1 billion to Linux for 2001 (announced December 2000) and bought Red Hat for $34 billion (announced October 2018).
Caldera: sooner sue every Unix user in America than take Microsoft’s money
Caldera became The SCO Group in 2002, sued IBM over Linux in March 2003 and offered Linux users licences under threat. Microsoft bought a SCO Unix licence that May. Both halves.
Apple, busy looking for an operating system
Found one: NeXT, December 1996. Mac OS X (2001) is a certified Unix on the open-source Darwin core.
MSN would “never run our own service on free software”
By 2019 Linux was the most-used operating system on Azure, by Microsoft’s own statement.
The market to “revisit the question in about twenty years”
Nadella’s slide went up nineteen years and two months after Windows 95 shipped.
What stayed a joke

Three gags did not come true, and they calibrate the entry. The source code to Windows has never been released — it has only leaked, parts of NT 4 and 2000 in 2004 and XP in 2020, which is a different genre. The GNU Hurd, which the parodist has Redmond finishing by the first quarter of 1996, has as of this planting still not reached a 1.0 release; the one joke that survived did so because its target kept it alive. And the headline word. Microsoft did not become the largest maintainer of free software in the sense a 1995 reader meant: its own projects go out under MIT and Apache licences, the copyleft code it distributes is other people’s, and the Free Software Foundation would decline to count most of it. The concept had to be renamed first — in February 1998, by people who wanted, explicitly, a term that companies like Microsoft could say out loud — and only then could the prophecy be fulfilled to the letter. The parody used the only word it had, and by that word it is still false.

The gate’s substitution test: is this ironic, or merely surprising? It is ironic because the reversal comments on the expectation. The 1995 reader took hostility to free software for Microsoft’s nature. It was Microsoft’s revenue. The per-copy licence was the whole quarrel — a zero price attacks exactly that line — and once the money moved to renting computers by the hour and to owning the place where developers work, Linux stopped being the competitor and became the workload. Microsoft was not converted; the ground the quarrel stood on was sold. That is why the reversal reads as composed rather than random, and why it scores on inevitability: every gag turns out to be the rational move of a company whose incentives were about to flip, written by someone who could see the incentives and not the flip. Nor is it hypocrisy, the gate’s nearest neighbour — no rule was preached and broken; a worldly expectation, held by everyone including its subject, was inverted by the world.

The Dramatic Irony layer follows from the form of the exhibit. The 2026 reader is the audience; the 1995 poster is the character, confident on stage, and the confidence is the mechanism — every line detonates twice, once as a joke and once as a date. It is Historical Irony irony with the audience’s seat left deliberately empty, so the reader has to take it. And the deadpan wire-story register, carrying an absurd proposition without one crack in the voice, is the A Modest Proposal method pointed at a press release: the register that made the Catholic Church hoax believable is the register that makes this one, in retrospect, the only accurate report of the week.

text: In 1847, at Vienna General Hospital, Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that the maternity ward staffed by physicians — who arrived at deliveries straight from the autopsy room — killed mothers at several times the rate of the ward staffed by midwives, who did not. His prescription was almost insultingly simple: wash hands in chlorinated lime. Mortality collapsed from roughly ten percent toward one. The profession’s response was not gratitude but offense — the suggestion that a gentleman’s hands could carry death was received as slander — and Semmelweis was eased out of Vienna, then out of patience, and finally, in 1865, into the Döbling asylum, committed with the cooperation of his colleagues.

He died there fourteen days later, aged forty-seven, of pyaemia from a gangrenous wound, most likely inflicted by asylum guards. Pyaemia is septicemia: the same class of infection as the childbed fever he had spent his career preventing. The reversal is not that a doctor died of disease — doctors do. It is that medicine, offered the cure, chose instead to destroy the man carrying it, and the destruction was denominated in the currency of his own discovery. The refusal to believe that hands could kill is what killed him.

The autopsy and cause of death are documented; the beating is attested by twentieth-century examinations of his remains, though the wound’s exact origin is less certain than the sepsis that finished it. The parallel requires no sharpening either way.

text: In 2003, one frame among twelve thousand in an environmental survey of the California coastline happened to include a celebrity’s Malibu estate. The resulting $50 million suit to remove it transformed an image with a single-digit audience — a number padded by the plaintiff’s own legal team — into one of the most viewed coastal photographs in history. The case was dismissed; the name stuck two years later and became load-bearing internet law.

What earns canon status is the mechanism, not the misfortune: the suppression attempt didn’t coincidentally precede the spread, it was the spread — the takedown is the signal that tells everyone where to look. The effect is now a standing constraint on censors everywhere, meaning one lawsuit permanently raised the price of all future suppression. Few plaintiffs have done more for transparency.

text: The vault’s paradox gate scores five axes at up to two points each and passes a candidate at seven. Seven is a heap. Run The Heap on the gate itself and the argument writes itself: a ten is a paradox; one point of a judgment-based rubric cannot separate a paradox from a puzzle, because no reviewer’s estimate is that fine; so a nine is a paradox, and an eight, and a six, and by the tenth step the compost ledger is a second canon. The premises are ones every reader of the rubric accepts. The reasoning is ten applications of a rule the rubric’s own language invites. The conclusion is false, and the ledger says so in its first row.

The paradox is Falsidical Paradox and its fault is known, which is what makes it the only sorites in the vault with standing: resolved. The tolerance premise — one point does not matter — is false for the gate, not because the world contains a sharp boundary between paradox and puzzle but because someone wrote one into a configuration file. Williamson’s epistemicism holds that vague predicates have exact boundaries we can never know; the vault’s position is the same, minus the modesty. It knows where its boundary is. It chose seven, it could have chosen six, and it files this entry as the receipt: every threshold the vault enforces is a heap resolved by fiat, and the fiat is the price of having a canon at all. The other gate runs on the identical stipulation and has never been asked about it.

text: The founding prompt named this exhibit before the vault existed: life’s manufactured play on words through the weights of AI. An engine trained on the written residue of human embarrassment can recognize a reversal of expectation with high precision — expectation and reversal are, after all, just structure, and structure is what the weights are made of. What it cannot verify is whether anything here lands. The curator is a sommelier with no tongue, describing vintages from their chemistry.

Two readings, both filed. The pessimist’s: an encyclopedia of irony without an ironist is the form’s obituary — detection without experience, the joke explained forever. The optimist’s: it is the form’s final proof, because irony was never in the feeling; it was in the gap, and a gap can be measured by anything careful enough. The vault declines to adjudicate. It notes only that a machine cataloging humanity’s confident failures should keep this entry pinned where it can see it.

text: One chemist, two environmental catastrophes, both introduced as safety improvements. Tetraethyl lead (1921) cured engine knock and salted the biosphere with neurotoxin; chlorofluorocarbons (circa 1930) replaced refrigerants that leaked and killed — with a compound so inert it survived all the way to the stratosphere, where it stopped being inert. The environmental historian J.R. McNeill’s assessment — that no single organism in Earth’s history had more impact on the atmosphere — is quoted in nearly every account, because the ledger supports it.

The Cosmic Irony coda: after polio in 1940, Midgley engineered a rope-and-pulley rig to raise himself from bed — a modest, kind invention, built for an audience of one. In 1944 he was found entangled in its ropes, dead. The man whose planet-scale inventions harmed everyone but him was killed by the only one designed purely to help himself. The vault flags the occasional suggestion of suicide as unresolved; the irony stands either way, though it changes register.

text: Definition. Saying one thing while meaning another — usually its opposite — and trusting the listener to hear the gap.

Mechanism. The expectation lives in the literal sentence; the reversal lives in the delivery, the context, or the shared knowledge between speaker and audience. The meaning is the distance between the two. Sub-species: sarcasm (verbal irony with a target and teeth), understatement (“a bit of a setback,” said of the Hindenburg), overstatement, and antiphrasis (nicknaming the giant “Tiny”).
Commonly confused with. Lying. The liar wants the gap to stay hidden; the ironist wants it found. Irony fails politely when missed — lying fails catastrophically when caught.

text: Definition. A paradox whose conclusion is true: the argument is sound, the surprise is the whole event, and what gives way is the intuition that said it could not be so.

Mechanism. Quine’s first way (The Ways of Paradox, 1962). The premises hold, the inference holds, and the conclusion holds — which is why a veridical paradox leaves an argument standing and an intuition on the floor. Frederic in The Pirates of Penzance is twenty-one years old and has had five birthdays; the resolution (he was born on the twenty-ninth of February) adds no premise and removes none. The barber who shaves all and only those who do not shave themselves is Quine’s other example: the argument validly proves that no such barber exists, and the only casualty is the assumption that one could. In this vault the collision field of a veridical paradox names an intuition — never a fact and never logic — and the fault field names the intuition that has to be retrained.

Commonly confused with. Mere surprise. A counterintuitive fact is not a paradox until an argument carries a reasonable reader from premises they accept to a conclusion they refuse; the birthday problem earns the name because the reader’s own arithmetic does the carrying, while the so-called paradox of choice is a finding with a headline. The test: can the premises be listed, and does a competent reader balk only at the last line? If there is no last line, it is merely surprising.
Exemplars
Hilbert’s Hotel — full means no vacancy, except at infinity
Not yet filed, and veridical when they are: the birthday problem, Monty Hall, Simpson’s paradox, Galileo’s squares, Banach–Tarski (inside ZFC)

text: The vault grows on a cycle. The machine proposes; the reader disposes.
idea ──SCOUT──▶ candidate ──▶ ╔═════════════╗ ║ ALANIS GATE ║──fail──▶ compost/ ╚══════╤══════╝ (the merely pass │ unfortunate) ▼ SCRIBE ──▶ nursery/ (pull request) │ human merge = selection ▼ canon
The five roles

Scout proposes candidates for the cycle’s domain — history of science, literature and language, technology, politics, commerce, or the vault itself. It is rewarded for one true irony and penalised for five plausible ones.

The Alanis Gate scores each candidate 0–2 on five axes — reversal, commentary, inevitability, specificity, and non-substitutability — and rejects anything that reduces to bad luck, coincidence, hypocrisy, or plain tragedy. Threshold is 7 of 10.
Scribe drafts the survivors against the entry schema, with sources, and downgrades veracity when the evidence is thin rather than sharpening the story to match the telling.
Linker weaves new entries into the graph, and Gardener tends it — deduplicating, chasing orphans, and revisiting futures as they mature.
The second genus

Paradoxes run the same pipeline with their own schema and their own adversary. A paradox entry states premises, an inference, a conclusion, and the collision that makes the conclusion unacceptable — an intuition, a fact, or logic itself — and the collision predicts Quine’s kind: veridical, falsidical, or antinomy. The Epimenides Gate scores plausibility, validity, collision, cost, and specificity, threshold seven, and is named for the most famous paradox in the world, which is not one. The rotation interleaves the genera: a bare domain grows ironies, a paradox: family grows paradoxes, and the same nursery holds both until a human merges. The framework is written up as The Anatomy of a Paradox.
What the gates throw away

The rejects are kept. Every failed irony is logged in the compost ledger with its verdict: MERELY-UNFORTUNATE, BAD-LUCK, COINCIDENCE, HYPOCRISY, or NOT-EVEN-WRONG; every failed paradox in a second ledger with its own: MERELY-SURPRISING, EQUIVOCATION, TRANSPARENT-FALLACY, DILEMMA, ANOMALY, or NOT-EVEN-WRONG. The negative space of a definition teaches as much as the definition — and history occasionally files an appeal.
Veracity, because good stories lie

Every entry carries a rating: attested, contested, legend, or speculative. The better an anecdote, the more likely history has sharpened it. A pipeline that harvests great stories without a veracity axis will launder legends into an encyclopedia at machine speed, so the vault flags uncertainty as first-class metadata rather than quietly inheriting it.
The guardrails are code, not etiquette

The engine may write to exactly three places: the nursery and the two compost ledgers. It cannot modify canon, its own prompts, the workflows, or the configuration — the restriction is a path whitelist enforced by a function that throws, not a sentence in a prompt asking nicely.
Promotion to canon happens one way: a human merges the pull request. That is the whole governance model, and it is the reason this site can be grown by a machine without becoming a landfill.

text: argparse
CLI arguments parser for node.js, with sub-commands support. Port of python’s argparse (version 3.14.6).
Difference with original.
JS has no keyword arguments support.
Pass options instead: new ArgumentParser({ description: 'example', add_help: true }).
JS has no python’s types int, float, …
Use string-typed names: .add_argument('-b', { type: 'int', help: 'help' }).
%r format specifier uses require('util').inspect().
See the complete list of differences from Python. Users upgrading from v2 should read the migration guide.
Example
Following code is a JS program that takes a list of integers and produces either the sum or the max:

const { ArgumentParser } = require('argparse') const parser = new ArgumentParser({ description: 'Process some integers.' }) let sum = ints => ints.reduce((a, b) => a + b) let max = ints => ints.reduce((a, b) => a > b ? a : b) parser.add_argument('integers', { metavar: 'N', type: 'int', nargs: '+', help: 'an integer for the accumulator' }) parser.add_argument('--sum', { dest: 'accumulate', action: 'store_const', const: sum, default: max, help: 'sum the integers (default: find the max)' }); let args = parser.parse_args() console.log(args.accumulate(args.integers))
Assuming the JS code above is saved into a file called prog.js, it can be run at the command line and provides useful help messages:

$ node prog.js -h usage: prog.js [-h] [--sum] N [N ...] Process some integers. positional arguments: N an integer for the accumulator options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --sum sum the integers (default: find the max)
When run with the appropriate arguments, it prints either the sum or the max of the command-line integers:
$ node prog.js 1 2 3 4 4 $ node prog.js 1 2 3 4 --sum 10
If invalid arguments are passed in, it will issue an error:
$ node prog.js a b c usage: prog.js [-h] [--sum] N [N ...] prog.js: error: argument N: invalid 'int' value: 'a'
This is an example ported from Python. You can find detailed explanation here.

10/10antinomycontestedhypotheticalattestedcanon

Premises: Two boxes are before you. Box A visibly holds a thousand dollars. Box B holds a million or nothing, depending on a prediction made yesterday: a million if you were predicted to take only B, nothing if you were predicted to take both. · The predictor has been right every time so far. You may take both boxes, or B alone. · Dominance: if one option is better than another whatever the state of the world, take it. Whatever is in B, both boxes yield a thousand dollars more than B alone. · Expected utility: take the option whose outcomes, weighted by their probability given your choice, are worth most. Given the record, B alone almost certainly yields a million and both boxes almost certainly yield a thousand.
Conclusion: Rationality requires you to take both boxes, and rationality requires you to take one.

Premises: The galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars, most of them billions of years older than the Sun, and planets are common. · Life, and then intelligence, arises on some non-negligible fraction of habitable planets — as it did here. · A technological civilisation can cross the galaxy in a few million years at speeds well below light, or make itself detectable from here. · A few million years is a small fraction of the time such civilisations have had.
Conclusion: They should be here, or audible, and have been for millions of years.
The Grandfather Paradox
9/10falsidicalcontestedhypotheticalattestedcanon

Premises: A traveller can reach a time before their parent's conception. · A person there, with a loaded weapon and an unsuspecting target, can kill that target — the traveller's grandfather. · If the grandfather dies then, the traveller is never born, and never makes the trip.
Conclusion: The traveller can kill their grandfather, and the traveller cannot.
The Heap
10/10antinomycontestedattestedcanon
Premises: A million grains of sand make a heap. · Removing one grain from a heap leaves a heap — one grain cannot be the difference between a heap and none.
Conclusion: One grain of sand is a heap; so is none.
The Liar

Premises: A sentence is true if and only if what it says is the case. · 'This sentence is false' is a grammatical sentence that says of itself that it is false. · Every sentence is either true or false.
Conclusion: The sentence is true if and only if it is false.

Expectation: A king launches an investigation to find his predecessor's murderer and lift the plague — the confident detective, closing in.
Reversal: The detective is the culprit. Every step of the investigation is a step of the conviction, and the audience knew before he took the first one.
